preamble: Debuccalization of the velar ejective: [kʼ] loses its oral closure and keeps only the glottal one, giving [ʔ]. Fallon (2002) counts this among the most frequent ejective changes, attested as regular or dialectal change in Chadic, Cushitic, Omotic, Athabaskan and Jicaquean. Several cases are still variable between dialects, showing the change in progress. Maltese, Cairene and urban Levantine Arabic reach ʔ in two steps, through uvular q (*kʼ > q > ʔ); each step is filed separately. In Athabaskan, stem-final *kʼ became ʔ in Navajo (*tsʼakʼʸ 'dish' > tsʼaaʼ), part of the loss of syllable-final ejectivity in the languages that developed tone; the Ahtna and Navajo words for 'three' (Proto-Athabaskan *taˑqʼə) continue the uvular ejective and belong to qʼ > ʔ. In North Omotic, Proto-Omotic *ḳ (= kʼ) gives ʔ in Yemsa and Wolaitta 'red', while Male and Oyda keep the ejective.

languageExamples.language: Hausa: Standard ƙ [kʼ] ~ East Hausa (Azare) ʔ (correspondence)

examples.note: Word-initial ƙ only (Dresel 1977, cited in Fallon 2002). The sources consulted give only this one example.
Western Jicaque kat instead lost the glottalization (Campbell & Oltrogge 1980).
Wikipedia (Jicaquean languages): proto-form from Campbell & Oltrogge (1980), daughter forms from Campbell (1999); Western Jicaque kaw- lost the glottalization instead.
Same table; Western Jicaque has te-ga. Word-finally Tol keeps the ejective: *sokʼ 'tail' > Tol sokʼ.

Stem-final position; Central Ahtna tsʼaayʼ has a glottalized glide instead. Wikipedia (Proto-Athabaskan language): nearly all languages that developed tone lost syllable-final ejectivity, keeping only glottalized sonorants and bare glottal stops in that position. Wiktionary also lists Krauss (1979) *cʼa̓ˑk̯ʼ; Leer's newer reconstruction reinterprets the traditional velars (*kʼ [kʼ]) as palatals (*kʼʸ [cʼ]). The sources consulted give only this one example.

Militarev's StarLing Omotic database, where ḳ is the velar ejective kʼ; Male and Oyda zoḳ- keep it. Bender (1988, cited in Fallon 2002) reconstructs *zokʼ and notes North Omotic zokʼ ~ zoʔ. The same database keeps ḳ in Wolaitta meḳetta 'bone' and queries the Yemsa form (<*ʒVḳw?), so the glottal stop in 'red' could depend on the following w. The sources consulted give only this one example.
